title: Arithmetic & Number Foundations
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Mathematics begins with numbers and operations. Number types: natural (1,2,3...), integers (...-1,0,1...), rational (fractions), irrational (√2, π — non-repeating decimals), and real numbers. The four operations and their properties: commutative (a+b=b+a), associative, distributive (a(b+c)=ab+ac). Order of operations (PEMDAS/BODMAS). Prime numbers are the building blocks — every integer factors uniquely into primes (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic). Fractions, decimals, percentages are three representations of the same idea: parts of a whole.

WORKED EXAMPLE: 3 + 4 × 2 = 11, not 14 — multiplication binds tighter than addition (order of operations). Getting 14 (adding first) is the single most common arithmetic error. The rules of precedence exist so every expression has exactly one correct value.

PRACTICE: 1) Factor 60 into primes. 2) Convert 3/8 to a decimal and percentage. 3) Evaluate 2 + 3 × (4 − 1)² using order of operations.

title: Algebra
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Algebra generalizes arithmetic using variables to represent unknowns. An equation is a balance — whatever you do to one side, do to the other. Solving linear equations isolates the variable. Exponents (repeated multiplication) and their laws (x^a · x^b = x^(a+b)). Polynomials, factoring, and the quadratic formula (x = (−b ± √(b²−4ac))/2a) solve second-degree equations. Functions map inputs to outputs — the core object of higher math. Graphing reveals structure: linear (straight), quadratic (parabola), exponential (rapid growth).

WORKED EXAMPLE: Solve 2x + 6 = 14. Subtract 6 from both sides: 2x = 8. Divide by 2: x = 4. Each step preserves the balance. Algebra's power is that this same logic solves for any unknown in any relationship, from physics to finance.

PRACTICE: 1) Solve 3x − 7 = 11. 2) Factor x² + 5x + 6. 3) Use the quadratic formula on x² − 4x + 3 = 0.

title: Geometry & Trigonometry
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Geometry studies shape, size, and space. Points, lines, angles, and the axioms of Euclid. Key results: angles in a triangle sum to 180°; the Pythagorean theorem (a² + b² = c² for right triangles). Area and volume formulas. Similarity and congruence. Trigonometry relates angles to side ratios: sine, cosine, tangent (SOH-CAH-TOA). The unit circle connects trig to rotation and periodicity. Coordinate geometry places shapes on axes, uniting algebra and geometry — a line becomes an equation.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A right triangle has legs 3 and 4. The hypotenuse = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5. The Pythagorean theorem — one of the oldest and most useful results in mathematics — lets you find any side of a right triangle from the other two, underpinning navigation, construction, and physics.

PRACTICE: 1) Find the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 5 and 12. 2) Calculate the area of a circle with radius 3. 3) Find sin, cos, tan of a 3-4-5 triangle's smallest angle.

title: Functions, Sequences & Precalculus
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: A function assigns each input exactly one output — the foundation of modeling change. Domain (valid inputs) and range (outputs). Function types: polynomial, rational, exponential (a^x — growth/decay), logarithmic (the inverse of exponential — how many times to multiply). Composition and inverse functions. Sequences (ordered lists) and series (their sums); arithmetic (constant difference) and geometric (constant ratio). Logarithms turn multiplication into addition — the key to compound growth, pH, decibels, and complexity analysis.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Exponential growth: $1,000 at 5% for 10 years = 1000 × (1.05)^10 ≈ $1,629. The exponent drives compounding. Logarithms answer the reverse: 'how long to double?' — log(2)/log(1.05) ≈ 14 years. Exponentials and logs are inverses that describe all growth and decay in nature and finance.

PRACTICE: 1) Evaluate log₂(8). 2) Find the 5th term of a geometric sequence starting at 3 with ratio 2. 3) Compute compound growth of $500 at 6% over 8 years.

title: Calculus
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Calculus is the mathematics of change and accumulation. Limits formalize 'approaching' a value. The derivative measures instantaneous rate of change (slope of a curve at a point) — velocity from position, marginal cost from cost. Rules: power rule, product, quotient, chain. The integral measures accumulation (area under a curve) — distance from velocity, total from rate. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus links them: differentiation and integration are inverse operations. Optimization (finding maxima/minima where the derivative is zero) is calculus's most practical application.

WORKED EXAMPLE: For f(x) = x², the derivative is f'(x) = 2x — at x=3, the curve's slope is 6. This means the function is changing 6 units per unit at that point. Setting a derivative to zero finds peaks and valleys, which is how businesses maximize profit and engineers minimize material — calculus turns 'find the best' into a solvable equation.

PRACTICE: 1) Differentiate f(x) = 3x². 2) Find where f(x) = x² − 6x has its minimum (set derivative = 0). 3) Explain what an integral accumulates.

title: Probability & Statistics
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Probability quantifies uncertainty (0 = impossible, 1 = certain). Independent vs dependent events; conditional probability P(A|B). Bayes' theorem updates beliefs with evidence — the foundation of rational inference and machine learning. Statistics extracts meaning from data: measures of center (mean, median, mode) and spread (variance, standard deviation). Distributions, especially the normal (bell curve) and the Central Limit Theorem (why averages are normally distributed). Correlation vs causation. Statistical inference: sampling, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, p-values, and their frequent misinterpretation.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A test is 99% accurate for a disease affecting 1 in 10,000. You test positive. Your actual chance of having it is only ~1%, not 99% — because false positives (99 per 10,000 healthy people) vastly outnumber the 1 true case. Bayes' theorem reveals this counterintuitive truth, which doctors and juries routinely get wrong. Base rates dominate.

PRACTICE: 1) Find the probability of two coin flips both landing heads. 2) Calculate the mean and standard deviation of {2,4,4,6}. 3) Explain why a positive test for a rare disease may still mean low probability of illness.

title: Grandmaster — Advanced & Applied Mathematics
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Higher mathematics builds powerful abstract structures. Linear algebra (vectors, matrices, transformations) underlies computer graphics, machine learning, and data science — a matrix is a function that transforms space. Differential equations model dynamic systems (populations, circuits, economies). Discrete mathematics (logic, sets, combinatorics, graph theory) is the mathematics of computing. Complex numbers (involving √−1) unify algebra and reveal deep structure. Multivariable calculus extends change to many dimensions. Abstract algebra studies structure itself (groups, rings, fields). These tools model nearly all of science and technology.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Machine learning trains a model by using linear algebra (matrix operations) and calculus (gradient descent — following the derivative downhill to minimize error) together. Every neural network is, at its core, matrices multiplied and derivatives computed billions of times. The 'AI' that seems magical is applied linear algebra and calculus at scale — the same tools taught here.

PRACTICE: 1) Explain what a matrix does geometrically (transforms space). 2) Describe gradient descent in plain terms. 3) Give an example of a system modeled by a differential equation.

title: King Level — The Nature and Frontier of Mathematics
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: At the highest level, mathematics is revealed as the study of pattern, structure, and truth itself — the language in which the universe appears to be written. Proof is its foundation: unlike science (which gathers evidence), mathematics establishes certainty through deductive proof from axioms. Gödel's incompleteness theorems show that any sufficiently powerful system contains true statements it cannot prove — a profound limit on formal knowledge. Open frontiers: the Riemann Hypothesis, P vs NP (whether hard problems are fundamentally hard — unsolved, and no clever architecture is known to beat it), and the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in describing reality. The King-level truth: mathematics is both invented (we choose axioms) and discovered (the consequences are not ours to decide) — and its deepest results reveal not just answers but the fundamental limits of what can be known or computed.

WORKED EXAMPLE: P vs NP asks whether every problem whose solution is easy to *check* is also easy to *solve*. Despite 50 years and a $1 million prize, it's unproven — and most mathematicians believe P ≠ NP, meaning some problems are inherently hard no matter how cleverly you approach them. This isn't a gap in our tools; it appears to be a fundamental feature of computation itself, bounding what any computer, however designed, can efficiently do.

PRACTICE: 1) Explain the difference between mathematical proof and scientific evidence. 2) Describe what Gödel's incompleteness theorem limits. 3) Explain in your own words why P vs NP matters for what computers can do.
